title: Navigating uncertain waters: a critical review of inferring foraging behaviour from location and dive data in pinnipeds

subsections.subsection_title: Physiological Foundations of Diving and Foraging Capacity
subsections.content:
The physiological capacity of pinnipeds to engage in prolonged and deep foraging dives is underpinned by specialized adaptations in oxygen storage and utilization. A hallmark of deep-diving mammals is the elevated concentration of myoglobin in skeletal muscle, which serves as the primary oxygen reservoir, accounting for more than 80% of total body oxygen stores in elite divers such as elephant seals and Weddell seals ref [1]. This muscular oxygen depot, combined with enhanced blood volume and hemoglobin concentration, enables extended aerobic dive durations, minimizing reliance on anaerobic metabolism—a strategy more common in diving birds ref [1]. The Weddell seal, for instance, exhibits exceptional aerobic endurance, with dive durations often exceeding the calculated aerobic dive limit, facilitated by efficient oxygen extraction and reduced metabolic rates during submersion ref [2].

Female northern elephant seals demonstrate a nearly continuous diving pattern during foraging migrations, with mean dive durations of nearly 20 minutes and depths reaching up to 894 m, indicating a physiological capacity to sustain prolonged aerobic activity under extreme pressure ref [3]. This behavior is energetically optimized, with short surface intervals (mean 2.8 min) allowing rapid reoxygenation and minimal time loss ref [3]. Foraging success is further linked to the duration spent at the bottom of dives, where accumulated bottom time correlates strongly with feeding events, suggesting that physiological limits on aerobic capacity directly constrain foraging efficiency ref [10]. Additionally, physiological constraints such as digestion and metabolic demand can temporarily reduce the aerobic dive limit, as observed in southern elephant seals feeding on benthic prey ref [4].

subsections.subsection_title: Instrumentation Effects and Ethical Considerations in Tagging
subsections.content:
The attachment of biologging instruments to pinnipeds can induce significant physiological and behavioral alterations, raising concerns about data validity and animal welfare. External devices increase drag, altering hydrodynamic efficiency and increasing energy expenditure during locomotion. Computational fluid dynamics simulations on grey seals demonstrated that satellite transmitters elevate drag coefficients by 12%, while also inducing substantial increases in pitching moment (32%) and lift (240%), potentially disrupting natural swimming mechanics and posture ref [7]. Experimental studies on Steller sea lions confirmed that drag, but not buoyancy, directly impairs swim speed, suggesting that tagged animals may suboptimally forage due to increased hydrodynamic costs ref [10].

Beyond hydrodynamics, visual and sensory stimuli from instrumentation can modify foraging behavior. Female Antarctic fur seals equipped with cameras and near-infrared flashes exhibited prolonged dive durations and altered diel dive patterns, with flash operation disrupting expected nighttime dive shallowing and increasing dive depth early in foraging trips ref [6]. These behavioral shifts, though within natural ranges, indicate that instrumentation may bias ecological inferences. Handling and tagging procedures themselves also induce stress responses, as evidenced in Antarctic fur seals where instrument attachment correlated with transient changes in haul-out behavior and energy allocation ref [8].

A comprehensive review of marine mammal tagging techniques highlights that while survival is rarely affected, short-term behavioral changes—including altered swimming, haul-out patterns, and maternal care—are frequently reported, yet underpublished due to publication bias ref [9]. Ethical frameworks must therefore prioritize minimally invasive designs, long-term monitoring of welfare indicators, and transparent reporting of both positive and negative outcomes to ensure scientific integrity and animal well-being.

subsections.subsection_title: Biologging Technologies for Monitoring Pinniped Behavior
subsections.content:
Biologging technologies have revolutionized the study of pinniped behavior by enabling high-resolution, continuous monitoring of movement, diving, and physiological responses in free-ranging individuals. Modern tags now integrate multiple sensors—such as accelerometers, conductivity-temperature-depth (CTD) recorders, and GPS/Argos transmitters—to capture fine-scale behavioral states and environmental context simultaneously. Accelerometry, in particular, has become a cornerstone for inferring foraging effort and body dynamics, with metrics like Overall Dynamic Body Acceleration (ODBA) serving as proxies for energy expenditure ref [13]. The development of CTD-Satellite Relay Data Loggers (CTD-SRDLs) has further expanded the utility of instrumented pinnipeds, allowing real-time collection of high-accuracy oceanographic profiles from remote and undersampled regions, effectively turning animals into autonomous oceanographic platforms ref [6]. These devices now routinely record temperature and salinity with precision better than 0.005 °C and 0.02, respectively, significantly enhancing both ecological and physical oceanography ref [6].

Beyond sensor innovation, advances in tag programming and data management have improved the fidelity of behavioral time-series data. Intelligent data loggers now employ context-driven compression and automated relay systems to maximize information yield while minimizing power consumption and tag size, enabling longer deployments on smaller species ref [7]. Crucially, the temporal frequency and spatial accuracy of location data are heavily influenced by programming protocols; irregular or infrequent sampling can obscure small-scale movement patterns, whereas frequent Argos fixes can compensate for lower positional accuracy when analyzed with state-space models ref [10]. The integration of biologging data with environmental datasets and advanced statistical frameworks has further refined behavioral inference, allowing researchers to link individual foraging decisions to broader ecological patterns ref [12].

subsections.subsection_title: Challenges in Spatial Accuracy and Data Interpretation
subsections.content:
Accurate spatial reconstruction of pinniped movements remains a fundamental challenge in inferring foraging behavior from satellite telemetry data. ARGOS location estimates, particularly for lower-quality classes (0, A, B), exhibit substantial spatial error, often exceeding 1 km and showing asymmetric biases between longitude and latitude ref [20]. Even with filtering, these errors can distort path geometry and misrepresent habitat use patterns, especially in coastal or complex bathymetric environments. The advent of Fastloc GPS has enabled direct validation of ARGOS accuracy, revealing that 68th percentile errors for ARGOS locations can range from 226 m (LC 3) to over 750 m (LC 1), with significant variability across species and habitats ref [16].

State-space models (SSMs) have been widely adopted to correct for these errors by incorporating movement dynamics, yet their performance remains context-dependent. Studies comparing SSM outputs against GPS ground truth show that while Kalman filtering and Bayesian SSMs improve location accuracy—reducing error by up to 27% compared to traditional least squares methods—their efficacy is sensitive to speed thresholds and sampling frequency ref [17], ref [18], ref [19]. Moreover, interpolated positions between satellite passes may introduce spurious movement patterns, particularly when animals exhibit rapid directional changes during foraging ref [8].

The spatial scale of behavioral inference is further compromised by the interaction between tracking error and analytical methods such as first-passage time (FPT) analysis, which is commonly used to detect area-restricted search. Spatial inaccuracies can reduce the probability of detecting ARS by over 50% across all scales, and require a minimum of 13 high-quality locations to reliably identify foraging zones—conditions rarely met with ARGOS-only data ref [8]. Consequently, misinterpretation of foraging effort remains a pervasive risk when spatial uncertainty is not explicitly quantified and accounted for in analytical frameworks.

subsections.subsection_title: Validating Foraging Inferences from Dive and Movement Data
subsections.content:
Validating foraging inferences from dive and movement data remains a central challenge in marine predator ecology, as indirect proxies such as dive duration, bottom time, and descent/ascent rates must be rigorously tested against direct measures of prey capture. Field validation using animal-borne video has emerged as a gold standard, demonstrating that descent rate alone can predict prey capture attempts (APCs) in Australian fur seals with up to 77.5% accuracy, and that the majority of dives contain successful captures ref [26]. Similarly, head-mounted accelerometers have been successfully calibrated against video to identify prey handling events with high precision, enabling the detection of fine-scale foraging behaviors in otariids ref [22]. These approaches have been extended to penguins, where supervised machine learning models using accelerometry classify prey capture events with 84.95% accuracy, validating the use of behavioral signatures beyond dive metrics ref [23].

For species where video is impractical, alternative proxies such as stomach temperature and jaw-motion recorders have provided critical validation. In northern elephant seals, stomach temperature drops confirmed feeding events, revealing that reduced transit rates correlate strongly with prey consumption, thereby supporting the use of movement metrics as indirect indicators ref [24]. Jaw-motion recorders further revealed that these seals make thousands of feeding attempts per foraging trip, primarily targeting small mesopelagic prey, challenging assumptions that deep dives equate to large prey captures ref [27]. A multi-scale analysis in Antarctic fur seals showed that predictive models of prey capture attempts improve with temporal aggregation, with descent and ascent rates being the most consistent predictors across scales, though model parameters vary by species and context ref [25]. Collectively, these studies underscore that while dive characteristics offer valuable proxies, their predictive power is context-dependent and must be validated against direct behavioral or physiological evidence.

subsections.section_title: Inferring Foraging Behaviour from Single Data Types
subsections.subsection_title: Inferring Foraging from Dive Profiles: Validations and Limitations
subsections.content:
Dive profiles have long served as a primary proxy for inferring foraging behavior in pinnipeds, with metrics such as bottom duration, descent/ascent rates, and dive shape commonly assumed to reflect foraging effort or success. However, these assumptions require empirical validation. Studies using animal-borne video and accelerometry have demonstrated that descent rate is a robust predictor of prey capture attempts in Australian fur seals, with models achieving up to 77.5% accuracy in classifying foraging dives ref [26]. Similarly, in Antarctic fur seals, descent and ascent rates at multiple temporal scales—ranging from individual dives to nightly periods—best predicted prey capture attempts, highlighting the scale-dependency of these relationships ref [25].

Dive shape classification further refines inference: U-shaped dives in harbour seals correlate with increased foraging activity, as validated by water-flux and video data, while V-shaped dives are associated with transit ref [28]. A novel broken-stick algorithm applied to high-resolution dive data revealed that foraging is not confined to the bottom phase but occurs in sinuous segments identified as 'hunting' phases, with 77% of prey capture attempts in southern elephant seals occurring within these segments ref [24]. Grey seals exhibit square-wave dives during short foraging trips, contrasting with V-shaped dives during transit, suggesting dive shape can distinguish behavioral states ref [10].

Yet limitations persist. Foraging may occur across multiple dive phases, and prey capture success does not always align with dive duration or shape ref [30]. Moreover, interspecific variation in diving physiology and prey capture mechanics means that models derived for one species often fail to generalize ref [11]. Three-dimensional movement analyses in ringed seals further show that local search behavior—critical to foraging—is best detected through spatial revisitation patterns, not depth-time profiles alone ref [16]. Thus, while dive profiles offer valuable insights, their utility as standalone proxies is constrained by behavioral complexity and ecological context.

subsections.section_title: Inferring Foraging Behaviour from Single Data Types
subsections.subsection_title: Direct Validation of Foraging Events Using Accelerometry and Video
subsections.content:
Direct validation of foraging events in pinnipeds has been significantly advanced through the integration of high-resolution head-mounted accelerometers and animal-borne video cameras. These technologies enable the precise identification of prey capture events by capturing the distinct kinematic signatures of feeding behaviors, such as rapid jaw movements and head jerks, which are often invisible to conventional dive or location data. Volpov et al. (ref [22]) demonstrated that accelerometry combined with video validation could accurately classify prey captures in Australian fur seals, identifying unique acceleration patterns associated with successful foraging attempts across diverse prey types. Similarly, Ydesen et al. (ref [33]) revealed that high-frequency (200–333 Hz) super-cranial accelerometry detected prey engulfment in harbour seals through distinct jerk signatures exceeding 1000 m s⁻³, distinguishing between raptorial and suction feeding modes with high fidelity.

Such approaches have since been extended to other pinniped species, including northern elephant seals and Steller sea lions, confirming the generalizability of acceleration-based feeding metrics across taxa. The temporal precision of these methods allows for the calibration of foraging proxies in archival tags, improving estimates of energy expenditure and foraging success in wild populations. Importantly, video validation remains critical for distinguishing true prey captures from non-foraging head movements, reducing false positives inherent in accelerometry-only analyses. Together, these multimodal techniques have established a gold standard for direct foraging inference, moving beyond correlative models to mechanistic understanding of predator-prey interactions in marine environments.

subsections.section_title: Inferring Foraging Behaviour from Single Data Types
subsections.subsection_title: Dive Behavior as a Proxy for Foraging Effort and Success
subsections.content:
Dive behavior has long been used as a proxy for foraging effort and success in pinnipeds, with metrics such as dive duration, depth, and inter-dive intervals interpreted as indicators of energy expenditure and prey encounter rates. However, these proxies must be validated against direct measures of foraging, as dive patterns can reflect resting, digestion, or thermoregulatory behaviors rather than active foraging. For instance, drift dives—characterized by passive, near-neutral buoyancy descent—have been shown in Baikal seals to coincide with prolonged surfacing periods, suggesting a combined function of food processing and rest rather than foraging itself, thereby complicating their use as direct foraging indicators ref [35]. Similarly, changes in drift rate during dives have been successfully linked to body condition in southern elephant seals, where declining buoyancy reflects blubber depletion over foraging trips, indirectly signaling energy gain or loss ref [36]. Stomach temperature telemetry provides a more direct measure of foraging success, revealing temporal feeding patterns and sex-specific differences in meal frequency and duration in grey seals, demonstrating that dive profiles alone may misrepresent actual foraging events ref [37].

Theoretical models further highlight the physiological trade-offs underlying dive behavior, showing that the allocation of time between aerobic and anaerobic metabolism influences foraging efficiency and dive cycle structure, with anaerobic dives potentially enabling deeper or longer foraging bouts at the cost of extended recovery ref [38]. Moreover, thermal and digestive constraints shape foraging behavior by limiting the rate and volume of prey intake, with digestion requiring substantial energy and blood flow that may compete with diving thermoregulation, thus forcing behavioral trade-offs ref [8]. In Southern Ocean predators, variations in dive behavior correlate with oceanographic conditions, suggesting that environmental context modulates the relationship between dive metrics and foraging outcomes ref [10]. Together, these studies underscore that while dive behavior offers valuable insights, its interpretation as a proxy for foraging effort or success requires integration with physiological, ecological, and behavioral validation.

subsections.section_title: Inferring Foraging Behaviour from Single Data Types
subsections.subsection_title: Spatial and Temporal Scales of Foraging Inference from Movement Data
subsections.content:
Inferring foraging behavior from movement data in pinnipeds requires careful consideration of both spatial and temporal scales, as foraging events occur across hierarchically structured environments. First-passage time (FPT) analysis has emerged as a key method to identify area-restricted search (ARS) by quantifying the time an animal spends within a given radius, thereby revealing the spatial scale at which search effort is concentrated ref [40]. However, the accuracy of FPT is highly sensitive to tracking resolution and environmental structure; spatial errors from Argos systems can reduce ARS detection probability by over 50%, particularly at scales below 10 km, though velocity filtering mitigates this effect ref [21]. Temporally, foraging behavior in marine predators like Antarctic fur seals operates at distinct scales—fine-scale foraging (intervals <5 min) reflects localized krill patch exploitation, while mesoscale movements (>5 min) indicate inter-patch travel, with these patterns varying interannually in response to prey distribution ref [9]. State-space modeling further enables the disentanglement of behavioral modes from noisy tracking data, allowing for robust identification of intensive versus extensive foraging phases that correlate with vertical dive activity and foraging success ref [11]. The integration of horizontal movement patterns with vertical dive data confirms that surface-based ARS can predict underlying foraging effort and success, as demonstrated in southern elephant seals ref [43].

Consequently, scale-dependent inference remains a critical challenge: too coarse a resolution obscures fine-scale foraging, while excessive detail may conflate movement noise with behavior. Optimal scale selection must account for tag error, sampling frequency, and ecological context, with FPT and state-space models offering complementary frameworks for multi-scale foraging inference in pinnipeds ref [40], ref [21], ref [43], ref [9], ref [11].

subsections.section_title: Inferring Foraging Behaviour from Single Data Types
subsections.subsection_title: Integrating Multi-Dimensional Data to Overcome Single-Data-Type Limitations
subsections.content:
Integrating multiple data streams—such as dive profiles, movement trajectories, and habitat variables—has emerged as a powerful strategy to overcome the inherent limitations of inferring foraging behavior from single data types. By combining horizontal movement metrics like path tortuosity with vertical dive characteristics, researchers can more accurately distinguish between transit and foraging states. For instance, ref [5] demonstrated that both accumulated bottom time and angular variance in movement paths significantly predicted feeding events in gray seals, highlighting the necessity of multi-dimensional modeling. Similarly, ref [44] developed a low-resolution dive index based on vertical sinuosity that effectively correlated with prey capture attempts, enabling foraging inference even from satellite-relayed data loggers with limited temporal resolution. Ref [5] further advanced this approach by integrating dive duration, depth, and post-dive surface intervals into a state-space model, revealing that foraging states in multiple pinniped species were best predicted by the interplay of horizontal and vertical movement dynamics, not by either dimension alone.

Such integrative frameworks not only improve the accuracy of foraging inference but also allow for scaling across temporal and spatial contexts, from individual bouts to entire foraging trips. The synergy between movement, diving, and environmental data enables the testing of more nuanced foraging theories that account for physiological constraints and habitat heterogeneity. Emerging methods now routinely fuse telemetry, accelerometry, and oceanographic data to generate probabilistic foraging likelihoods, moving beyond binary classifications toward continuous estimates of foraging effort and success.

Environmental variability and climate-driven oceanographic shifts profoundly influence pinniped foraging behavior by altering prey distribution, abundance, and accessibility. Long-term studies on Antarctic fur seals (Arctocephalus gazella) demonstrate that interannual fluctuations in sea-surface temperature and the position of the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone directly affect foraging zone selection, diving depth, and pup provisioning efficiency, with extreme events like the 1997–1998 El Niño significantly reducing foraging success ref [46]. Similarly, southern elephant seals exhibit reduced juvenile survival during periods of low Southern Oscillation Index (SOI), indicating that large-scale climate anomalies cascade through trophic levels to impact demographic outcomes ref [13]. Climate-mediated changes in primary productivity and mesopelagic prey fields also reshape foraging landscapes for harbor seals, where regional habitat constraints and prey availability, rather than individual traits, dictate movement patterns ref [11].

Temporal and spatial variation in survival rates of Hawaiian monk seals further underscores the pervasive influence of climate variability, with synchronized declines across subpopulations suggesting regionally coherent environmental stressors ref [15]. The integration of animal-borne CTD-SRDLs has revolutionized the ability to link individual foraging behavior to fine-scale oceanographic conditions, enabling real-time monitoring of thermal structure and salinity gradients that correlate with prey aggregation ref [10]. Collectively, these findings reveal that climate impacts are not uniform but are mediated by local oceanography, prey dynamics, and species-specific life-history traits. As climate change accelerates, predictive models must incorporate multi-scale environmental drivers and their interactions with intrinsic factors to accurately forecast population responses ref [48].

subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Integration: Linking Behavior to Environment
subsections.content:
Integrating movement behavior with environmental context requires statistical frameworks that explicitly link latent behavioral states to external conditions. Hidden Markov models (HMMs) have emerged as a powerful tool for this purpose, enabling the simultaneous inference of behavioral states from telemetry data and their covariation with environmental variables such as sea surface temperature or bathymetry ref [52]. By modeling state transitions as functions of environmental covariates, HMMs move beyond descriptive classification to mechanistic interpretation, allowing researchers to test hypotheses about how habitat features drive foraging decisions in pinnipeds. Complementary approaches, such as mixture models of random walks, further enhance this integration by assigning movement steps to distinct behavioral modes—e.g., encamped versus exploratory—while incorporating habitat type as a predictor of state switching ref [51]. These methods are particularly valuable for pinnipeds, whose foraging behavior is often cryptic and spatially heterogeneous.

Beyond state classification, frameworks for estimating space-use and habitat preference from telemetry data provide a broader context for linking behavior to environment, treating usage as a function of environmental availability and selection ref [5]. This approach allows for the derivation of preference functions that account for spatio-temporal autocorrelation and unbalanced sampling, critical challenges in marine telemetry. When combined with dive and accelerometry data, such models can distinguish between habitat use driven by foraging effort versus transit, improving the ecological interpretability of movement patterns. Recent advances in Bayesian hierarchical modeling further enable the fusion of multiple data streams—GPS locations, oceanographic sensors, and dive profiles—into unified inference frameworks that quantify the relative influence of environmental drivers on behavioral state probabilities.

Tidal currents significantly shape the spatial foraging habitat use of pinnipeds by modulating prey distribution and hydrodynamic conditions that enhance foraging efficiency. Harbour seals (Phoca vitulina) in coastal channels exhibit strong fidelity to narrow constrictions during flood tides, where prey aggregation and increased water flow facilitate ambush predation, as demonstrated by high seal densities and peak foraging activity during incoming tides ref [55]. Similarly, in the San Juan Islands, harbour seals concentrate foraging efforts near tidal channel constrictions during flooding, with higher capture rates of salmon and schooling forage fish observed under slower flood currents, indicating that hydrographic features act as functional foraging corridors ref [54]. These patterns are not uniform across species or life stages; Australian sea lion juveniles, for instance, restrict their movements to shallower coastal waters with limited tidal exposure, suggesting ontogenetic constraints on spatial habitat use and reduced access to deeper, tidally influenced foraging zones ref [5].

The interaction between tidal phase and bathymetry creates predictable spatiotemporal hotspots that pinnipeds exploit, with telemetry data revealing repeated use of specific topographic features across tidal cycles. This behavioural plasticity allows individuals to optimize energy intake by aligning movement with prey availability driven by tidal dynamics. However, the reliance on such predictable corridors may render populations vulnerable to anthropogenic alterations in coastal hydrodynamics or prey phenology, particularly for younger or less mobile individuals with restricted foraging ranges. Future studies integrating high-resolution telemetry with hydrodynamic modelling are needed to quantify how tidal modulation of habitat use scales across life histories and geographic regions.

Oceanographic features such as thermal and chlorophyll-a fronts, eddies, and current interfaces play a pivotal role in structuring foraging habitats for pinnipeds by concentrating prey through physical aggregation mechanisms. Studies on basking sharks and pelagic seabirds have demonstrated that mesoscale fronts serve as predictable foraging hotspots, where zooplankton and small fish accumulate due to convergent flows and nutrient upwelling, a pattern increasingly recognized in marine mammals ref [59], ref [60]. Southern elephant seals from the Kerguelen Islands exhibit targeted foraging behavior along the Polar Front and near the Antarctic continent, where distinct temperature signatures correlate with increased dive density and improved body condition, suggesting fine-scale selection of oceanographic niches ref [7]. Similarly, bottlenose dolphins in the Moray Firth concentrate foraging efforts near small-scale hydrographic fronts and steep bathymetric gradients, optimizing energy efficiency by exploiting prey concentrated by tidal and topographic interactions ref [58]. Neglecting ocean current effects on animal movement trajectories can misidentify foraging zones, as drift and advection may mask true behavioral patterns, underscoring the necessity of integrating in situ current data with tracking datasets ref [57]. Recent advances in composite front mapping using Earth Observation data have enabled high-resolution quantification of these associations, revealing that pinnipeds often select regions with sharp thermohaline gradients that enhance prey encounter rates ref [39].

The interaction between oceanographic drivers and pinniped foraging is further modulated by species-specific foraging strategies and depth preferences. For instance, benthic foragers may target colder bottom waters near continental shelves, while pelagic foragers prefer warmer, frontal zones, indicating adaptive responses to prey distribution shaped by hydrodynamics ref [7]. These patterns are not static; interannual variability in oceanographic conditions, such as shifts in front position or intensity, can alter foraging success and drive changes in movement patterns across populations ref [39]. Integrating biologging data with high-resolution oceanographic models is therefore essential to disentangle intrinsic behavioral decisions from extrinsic environmental forcing, ultimately improving predictions of foraging habitat under climate-driven ocean change.

subsections.subsection_title: Intrinsic Factors: Sex, Age, and Body Condition
subsections.content:
Intrinsic factors such as sex, age, and body condition profoundly influence foraging behavior in pinnipeds, shaping spatial patterns, dive profiles, and energy allocation strategies. Sex-specific differences are well documented, particularly in size-dimorphic species like the grey seal, where males and females exhibit distinct foraging tactics linked to reproductive roles: females prioritize energy accumulation for pregnancy and lactation, resulting in longer, deeper dives and more consistent foraging effort before parturition, while males show more uniform, less seasonally variable diving behavior ref [68]. These behavioral divergences are mirrored in diet composition, with adult females selecting higher-energy prey during critical post-breeding periods, whereas males exhibit broader dietary niche breadth ref [67]. Body size further modulates foraging efficiency, as larger individuals—particularly in harbour seals—undertake longer foraging trips with greater ranges, suggesting enhanced capacity for energy acquisition ref [63].

Ontogeny plays a critical role in foraging development, with juveniles exhibiting prolonged trip durations, greater transit times to foraging grounds, and less efficient spatial use compared to adults, indicative of learning curves and physiological constraints ref [65]. In grey seal pups, age at weaning strongly predicts early dive performance, while body mass influences peak diving capacity and long-term survival, revealing a trade-off between developmental timing and energetic reserves ref [9]. Similar patterns emerge in Galapagos sea lions, where juvenile foraging strategies evolve over 18 months, with environmental stressors like El Niño further delaying independence ref [8]. Collectively, these intrinsic factors interact with life-history stages to determine foraging success, with sex and body condition often mediating responses to environmental variability, necessitating their explicit integration in behavioral inference models ref [62].

Figures and tables in pinniped foraging studies serve as critical tools for visualizing complex movement, dive, and environmental datasets, enabling the interpretation of latent foraging behaviors. Heatmaps of dive depth and duration, overlaid with oceanographic layers, have been instrumental in identifying foraging hotspots linked to mesoscale fronts and bathymetric features [42, 34]. Time-series plots of accelerometry and stomach temperature data have successfully revealed prey capture events, validating inferences drawn from dive shape analysis [55, 53]. First-passage time (FPT) maps, often presented as spatial heatmaps, effectively delineate area-restricted search behavior across varying spatial scales, though their accuracy depends on tracking resolution and environmental heterogeneity [5, 66]. State-space models, frequently visualized through posterior probability plots, help disentangle behavioral states from noisy location data, improving the reliability of inferred foraging zones [13, 48].

Tables summarizing dive parameters by sex, age, or season are essential for highlighting intraspecific variation, such as differences in dive duration or bottom time linked to body mass or reproductive status [12, 23]. However, inconsistent reporting of metrics—such as whether dive profiles are mean, median, or mode—can hinder cross-study comparisons. Recent advances in multivariate visualization, including 3D movement trajectories and dynamic habitat corridors, have enhanced the depiction of foraging behavior in relation to tidal and current dynamics [26, 65]. Standardization of figure legends and table metadata is increasingly advocated to improve reproducibility and meta-analytic potential [44, 47].
